title: Matthew 22:15–22
context: Pharisees and Herodians try to trap Jesus on the poll tax. His answer—“render to Caesar… and to God”—exposes bad faith, affirms civil duty without surrendering worship, and leaves opponents marveling as Passion Week tension rises.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: On Pharisees and Herodians try to trap Jesus on the poll tax, a few classic voices from each tradition.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: The Herodians were a set of men peculiarly attached to Herod, and consequently zealous for the interest of the Roman government, which was the main support of the dignity and royalty of his family. Thou regardest not the person of men - Thou favourest no man for his riches or greatness.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on Matt 22:15–22)

reformed.quote: That they might entrap him in his words. The Pharisees, perceiving that all their other attempts against Christ had been fruitless, at length concluded that the best and most expeditious method of destroying him was, to deliver him to the governor, as a seditious person and a disturber of the peace.
reformed.source: Commentary on a Harmony of the Evangelists (on Matt 22:15–22)

verses.text: Then the Pharisees went and took counsel how they might entrap him in his talk.
verses.arminianNotes:
Opposition turns tactical: they plot to entangle Jesus in speech. Hostile intent meets the Teacher who still speaks truth in public.

Classical Arminians note that light keeps shining amid schemes. Grace does not withdraw from contested spaces; Jesus remains available to be heard rightly even when hearers aim to trap Him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Matthew names the plot: Pharisees seek to entangle Him in His words. Human conspiracy advances toward the cross under a darker wisdom than theirs.

Reformed readers see providence over malice. Their plotting is sin, yet it cannot outrun the Father’s purpose for the Son in this week.

verses.text: They sent their disciples to him, along with the Herodians, saying, “Teacher, we know that you are honest, and teach the way of God in truth, no matter whom you teach; for you aren’t partial to anyone.
verses.arminianNotes:
Flattery opens the trap: they call Him true, God’s truthful teacher, unmoved by appearances. The compliments are accurate in form, hollow in motive.

Grace can be praised with the lips while the heart resists. True teaching still deserves honest approach, not staged praise that softens a snare.
verses.reformedNotes:
Disciples of the Pharisees arrive with Herodians—an odd alliance—armed with polished flattery.

God is not fooled by speech. Their confession that Jesus teaches God’s way truthfully will rebound; the One they flatter is the Truth who will unmask them.

verses.text: Tell us therefore, what do you think? Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not?”
verses.arminianNotes:
The question forces a binary: lawful to pay Caesar’s tax, or not? Either answer seems to cost Him—Rome or the crowd.

Arminian interpreters hear a moral query buried under bad faith. God’s law addresses civic life; Jesus will answer without surrendering the kingdom’s claim on the conscience.
verses.reformedNotes:
“Is it lawful…?” is designed as a no-win. Politics and piety are weaponized against the Messiah.

No dilemma escapes Christ’s wisdom. The question He is asked sits inside the hour God appointed for revealing His lordship over Caesar and conscience.

verses.text: But Jesus perceived their wickedness, and said, “Why do you test me, you hypocrites?
verses.arminianNotes:
Jesus knows their malice and names the test: hypocrisy. Grace includes exposing false motives so repentance remains possible.

The Lord still addresses them—“Why do you test me?”—a searching word that invites honesty rather than only condemnation.
verses.reformedNotes:
Awareness of malice precedes the answer. He labels them hypocrites—truth-telling judgment.

Christ’s knowledge is perfect; their hearts are open before Him. The rebuke is just and serves the revealing work of this Passion week.
verses.keyContrast: Both affirm Jesus’ true discernment of malice. Arminians typically underline a searching rebuke that still summons honesty; Calvin’s heirs generally press the same holy exposure as certain knowledge advancing God’s purpose in the confrontation.

verses.text: Show me the tax money.” They brought to him a denarius.
verses.arminianNotes:
He asks for the tax coin; they produce a denarius. The object lesson begins with what they already handle.

Classical Arminians note ordinary means: Jesus teaches with a coin in hand. Grace meets people in the currency of their daily compromises and calls for clear thinking.
verses.reformedNotes:
“Show me the” turns their trap into a classroom. They bring the denarius without delay.

Even the props of the test serve the Teacher. God orders the moment so the image on the coin will preach.

verses.text: He asked them, “Whose is this image and inscription?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jesus asks whose image and inscription the coin bears. He draws the answer from them. Image-language echoes Genesis: coins bear Caesar’s image; people bear God’s.

Arminian teaching loves this hinge: rightful claims follow likeness. Civic tokens and divine image both matter—neither cancels the other.
verses.reformedNotes:
The question is precise: likeness and inscription. Authority is tied to whose image marks the object.

Reformed theology hears creation and providence: Caesar’s coin, God’s image-bearers. Christ frames the whole ethic before He states the duty.

verses.text: They said to him, “Caesar’s.” Then he said to them, “Give therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.”
verses.arminianNotes:
They concede “Caesar’s”; Jesus replies with the double render: give Caesar his due, and God His. Civil obligation stands; worship and ultimate allegiance remain God’s alone.

Classical Arminians stress responsible freedom under grace: believers may pay tax without idolizing the state, and must yield themselves—image-bearers—to God. Both duties are true.
verses.reformedNotes:
“Render to Caesar… and to God” is kingdom wisdom in one sentence. Earthly authority receives its limited due; God receives what is inalienably His.

Christ upholds ordered spheres under God’s sovereignty. Paying the tax does not shrink God’s claim; rendering to God relativizes Caesar without anarchic revolt.
verses.keyContrast: Both receive the double command as true. Arminians typically stress believers’ responsibility in both civic duty and wholehearted yielding to God; Reformed readers stress the same duties under Christ’s lordship and God’s sovereign ordering of earthly authority.

verses.text: When they heard it, they marveled, and left him and went away.
verses.arminianNotes:
They marvel—and leave. Amazement without repentance is possible; the trap fails, yet hearts may still walk away.

Marveling at Jesus’ wisdom is not the same as trusting Him. Grace gave a clarifying word; the next step is to stay and obey, not merely exit impressed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Marvel, then departure. The plot collapses under His answer.

God frustrates the snare and still leaves room for later hardening. Their exit does not undo Christ’s victory in the exchange; the week moves on toward the cross He came to bear.
